title: RFID Card Cost Guide — Chip, Material and Volume Price Breakdown
summary: A finished RFID card runs US$0.30-0.70 for MIFARE Classic 1K in PVC at volume, up to US$2-6+ for premium bodies with high-security chips. Those are industry-reference ranges assembled from Proud Tek's published guides and independent 2026 pricing reports, not a Proud Tek quote. Four levers set the price: chip/security tier, substrate material, order volume, and personalization; a 50,000-unit committed order runs 30-50% below a 1,000-unit pilot per card.
heroPoints: Four levers set the price of an RFID card, in order of impact: chip/security tier (a bare LF chip and a DESFire EV3 secure chip can differ 10x in cost), substrate material (virgin PVC to premium wood is roughly a 4-8x spread), order volume (500-unit pilots typically price 40-60% higher per card than 100,000-unit runs), and personalization (printing, pre-encoding, packaging each add small per-card increments that compound at scale).

As a directional anchor: a basic MIFARE Classic 1K PVC access card in volume lands somewhere in the US$0.30-0.70 range fully finished; a premium wood or polycarbonate card with a high-security DESFire or NTAG 424 DNA chip can run US$2-6+. Every number in this guide is a reference range assembled from Proud Tek's own published chip and material cost data plus independent industry pricing reports — treat it as a planning band, not a quote.

The fastest way to get from 'reference range' to 'real number' is the interactive cost estimator, which applies these same tables to your specific chip, material and volume selection, or a direct RFQ with your exact specification.

sections.title: The four cost levers, and which one to fix first
sections.intro: RFID card pricing looks opaque from the outside because quotes vary 10x or more between two cards that look identical on a spec sheet. In practice only four variables matter, and they stack multiplicatively rather than by simple addition. Fixing the two levers procurement actually controls — chip tier and volume commitment — before shopping quotes removes most of the apparent noise between supplier bids.
bullets: Chip / security tier is the single largest lever. A bare LF proximity chip with no cryptography and a DESFire EV3 chip with AES-128 mutual authentication are both '13.56 MHz-ish RFID chips' to a non-specialist, but the silicon cost alone can differ by an order of magnitude, before the card body is even added. Security tier should be the first decision, driven by threat model (see the MIFARE Classic vs Plus vs DESFire comparison), not by habit or whatever the incumbent supplier already stocks.

Substrate / card-body material is the second lever. Virgin PVC is the cost floor; recycled PVC, PET and bio-composite carry a modest premium; wood, bamboo and polycarbonate carry a much larger one. Material choice is usually a brand/sustainability/durability decision more than a technical one, so it is worth deciding after chip tier, not before — a premium wood body wrapped around a chip that does not match the application's actual security need is a common overspend.

Order volume is the lever with the most compounding effect and the one buyers most often leave on the table. Standard published price breaks sit around 500-1,000 units (pilot), 5,000-10,000 units (first production run), and 50,000-100,000+ units (established programme). Moving from a 1,000-unit pilot to a 50,000-unit committed order routinely drops per-card cost 30-50%, independent of any change to chip or material.

Personalization and finishing are the smallest individual levers but the ones buyers most often forget to budget. Full-color CMYK printing, pre-encoding (loading facility-specific keys/data before the card ships instead of on-site), holographic or UV-ink anti-counterfeit features, and branded packaging/sleeves each add a few cents per card — negligible on a 500-card order, materially additive across 100,000 cards.

How to use this guide: read the chip-tier table to pick a security level, the material table to pick a card body, apply the volume discount curve, then add whichever finishing options the programme actually needs. The interactive estimator below runs this same four-step logic and returns a single reference range for your combination.

sections.title: Chip and security tier — cost ladder from bare LF to high-security NFC
sections.intro: Chip selection is where the widest cost spread lives, because it is really a security-tier decision wearing a frequency label. Below is the cost ladder from least to most expensive, anchored to Proud Tek's own published chip encyclopedia figures where available and general market reference ranges elsewhere.
bullets: LF proximity (125 kHz — EM4100/EM4200, T5577): the cost floor of the category. No cryptography, read-only or simple read/write, used for low-risk proximity access (gyms, low-security office, legacy migrations). Bare chip-on-card cost is typically well under US$0.10 at volume; this tier is chosen for cost and legacy-reader compatibility, not security — see the LF chip encyclopedia for the full command/memory reference and the honest security posture (clonable in seconds with a US$20-50 consumer duplicator, per the same guide).

HF/NFC entry tier (MIFARE Ultralight, Ultralight C, NTAG 213): the next step up, still no or minimal cryptography. MIFARE Ultralight Nano (bare-bones, 40-byte memory) targets roughly US$0.03-0.05 at 10M-unit volumes; Ultralight C (with 3DES authentication) runs closer to US$0.32 per finished card at moderate volumes (the price IHG's approved supplier list shows in stock). NTAG 213 chip-only pricing runs roughly US$0.04-0.08 at 100K volumes. This tier suits single-use tickets, loyalty cards and low-risk NFC tap use cases.

HF/NFC standard tier (MIFARE Classic 1K/4K): the most widely deployed access-control and hotel-keycard chip family worldwide, despite the CRYPTO-1 cipher having been fully broken since 2008 (see the MIFARE Classic chip encyclopedia). Authentic NXP silicon through authorised distribution runs roughly US$0.11-0.18 per inlay; suspiciously cheap US$0.06-0.08 pricing on the open Shenzhen spot market is a known signal for Fudan or Huahong clone die printed in NXP packaging, not a legitimate volume discount — verify chip origin for any access-control or hospitality deployment.

HF/NFC high-security tier (MIFARE Plus SE, MIFARE DESFire EV2/EV3, NTAG 424 DNA): AES-128 mutual authentication and, for NTAG 424 DNA, per-tap dynamic message authentication (SUN/CMAC) for tamper-evident NFC. Chip-on-tape for NTAG 424 DNA runs roughly US$0.18-0.28 per die at 100K quantities; DESFire EV3 in finished-card form typically prices 3-6x a Classic 1K card of the same body. This tier is the correct default for any new-build hotel, finance-adjacent, government or brand-authentication programme — see the NTAG 424 DNA authentication guide for why the dynamic-tag feature specifically matters for anti-counterfeit use cases.

UHF and dual-frequency cards: pure UHF cards (for long-range access or asset-style tracking on a card form factor) use the same chip families covered in the UHF reader/tag pricing context — NXP UCODE 8/9, Impinj Monza R6-P, Alien Higgs 9 — typically in the US$0.15-0.40 chip-cost range depending on tier. Dual-frequency (LF+HF) cards, used in phased lock-migration programmes where legacy LF back-of-house access has to keep working alongside new HF guest-room locks, add a US$0.80-1.50 premium per card over a single-frequency equivalent for the second antenna/chip and the more complex lamination.

A note on 'too good to be true' pricing: across every tier, a quote meaningfully below the ranges above for an otherwise-identical spec is the single most common early warning sign of counterfeit or grey-market silicon, not a manufacturing efficiency the quoting supplier has found that authorised-channel suppliers have not. This matters most for MIFARE Classic (widely counterfeited) and matters least for LF chips (low value, less counterfeiting incentive).

sections.title: Substrate and card-body material — cost ladder from virgin PVC to polycarbonate
sections.intro: Once chip tier is fixed, the card body is the next lever. Reference figures below are typically quoted per finished card (chip + body + basic single-color print) at a 10,000-unit volume unless noted, drawn from Proud Tek's own hotel-keycard material selection guide.
bullets: Virgin PVC — the cost floor for a serious commercial card: roughly US$0.28-0.45 per card at 10,000-unit volume. The default choice when the per-card cost ceiling is under US$0.10-0.15 for the body alone (leaving budget for chip and finishing).

Recycled PVC — a modest sustainability upgrade at a modest premium: 60%-recycled content runs roughly US$0.35-0.55, 90%-recycled roughly US$0.40-0.60. The recycled-content premium over virgin PVC is rarely more than 20-30%, which is why recycled PVC is usually the default 'greener' swap rather than a full material change.

Premium wood (bamboo, walnut and similar): roughly US$1.20-3.50 per card at 10,000-unit volume, bamboo at the low end and walnut at the high end (one sourcing reference puts premium wood as high as US$1.80-3.50 depending on finish). A 4-8x premium over virgin PVC, generally justified for boutique/luxury hospitality positioning where average daily rate supports the delta, and rarely justified for a large convention property where the card is a high-volume consumable.

Polycarbonate (Teslin-core or solid PC with laser-engraved personalisation): roughly US$2.40-6.20 per card at 5,000+ unit volumes. Used where the card is a durable, long-lived, individually-issued credential (employee badge, university/government ID, aviation crew credential) rather than a high-turnover consumable — 5,000-10,000+ issuance cycles and 5-10 years of service versus 1,000-3,000 cycles and 2-4 years for standard PVC.

Framing the decision: the practical procurement question is 'what is the per-card cost ceiling the program can absorb, given expected replacement/reissue rate?' Below roughly US$0.10 for the body, only virgin or recycled PVC survive. In the US$0.10-0.30 body-cost range, recycled PVC, PET and the least expensive wood (bamboo) become viable. Above roughly US$0.30 for the body, the full material menu opens, including premium wood and polycarbonate.

sections.title: Volume breaks — how order size compounds with chip and material choice
sections.intro: Volume is the lever most likely to be under-optimized by first-time buyers, because the discount curve is steep and non-linear rather than a flat percentage-per-thousand-units. The bands below are consistent with both Proud Tek's own hotel-keycard sourcing figures and independent 2026 industry benchmarking of RFID tag/card procurement.
bullets: Pilot tier (500-1,000 units): expect list or near-list per-unit pricing. This tier is correctly treated as a sampling/validation cost, not a representative unit economics figure — do not budget a full-programme rollout off pilot-tier per-card pricing.

First-production tier (5,000-10,000 units): the first meaningful discount band. Most of the specific figures in this guide's chip and material sections are anchored to this tier, since it is the most commonly quoted volume in supplier RFQs and Proud Tek's own published references.

Established-programme tier (50,000-100,000+ units): independent industry benchmarking on RFID tags/cards broadly documents 40-60% cost reduction between minimum-order-quantity pricing (500-1,000 units) and high-volume pricing (100,000+ units) — consistent with the discount curve Proud Tek's own hotel-keycard and wristband sourcing data shows at comparable volume steps.

Consolidation matters as much as raw volume: buyers who order the same card spec across multiple properties, departments or locations independently routinely leave the volume discount on the table entirely, because no single order crosses the next price-break threshold. Centralizing procurement into fewer, larger purchase orders — even across otherwise-unrelated business units — is one of the highest-leverage, zero-technology cost reductions available.

Standardizing the chip/material spec across a portfolio (rather than customizing per-property or per-department) compounds with volume consolidation: fewer distinct SKUs means every order contributes to the same price break instead of splitting volume across variants that each individually stay in a lower discount tier.

sections.title: Personalization, encoding and finishing add-ons
sections.intro: The smallest line items on a per-card basis, and the ones most often left out of a first budget pass because each one looks negligible in isolation.
bullets: Custom full-color CMYK printing: the baseline expectation for any brand-facing card today (hotel keys, membership, loyalty, Google Review NFC cards) rather than a premium add-on. Cost is normally already folded into the finished-card prices quoted above rather than itemized separately, but single-color or blank-stock cards can run 10-20% below a fully custom-printed equivalent.

Pre-encoding: loading facility-specific keys, sector data or access credentials onto the card during manufacturing instead of on-site at check-in or issuance. Typically adds US$0.05-0.15 per card for partial pre-encoding and US$0.15-0.35 for full pre-encoding with key injection. At meaningful volume (50,000 cards/year, per Proud Tek's own hotel-encoding guide) full pre-encoding runs an incremental US$7,500-17,500/year against the base card cost — usually paid back within a year through faster check-in throughput and reduced front-desk encoder wear.

Anti-counterfeit and tamper-evident finishing: micro-text, guilloche patterns, UV-reactive ink and optically-variable ink are each modest per-card additions individually, more relevant to luxury/high-value brand cards than to operational access cards. Combine with a high-security chip tier (DESFire, NTAG 424 DNA) rather than substituting for one — printed anti-counterfeit features protect the visual brand, not the credential.

Packaging and sleeves: branded sleeves typically add US$0.03-0.08 per card plus 1-2 weeks of lead time (a separate print job); plain sleeves cost less but lose the branded unboxing moment; loose/unsleeved cards save the most but risk handling damage in transit and complicate hand-count verification on receipt.

Serialization / unique numbering: sequential or randomized per-card serial encoding (distinct from the chip's own factory-programmed unique ID) is typically a small fixed setup fee plus a negligible per-card increment, and is standard practice for any card tracked in an access-control, membership or loyalty database.

faq.question: How much does an RFID card cost per unit?
faq.answer: It depends primarily on chip security tier, card body material and order volume. As a directional reference range: a basic LF proximity or entry-level NFC card in PVC at volume can land under US$0.20 finished; a standard MIFARE Classic 1K PVC access card typically runs US$0.30-0.70 finished; a high-security DESFire EV3 or NTAG 424 DNA card, or a premium wood or polycarbonate body, can run US$2-6+. These are industry-reference ranges assembled from Proud Tek's own published chip and material cost data plus independent 2026 industry pricing reports, not a quote — use the cost estimator or request a quote for a number specific to your exact spec.

faq.question: What is the biggest lever for reducing RFID card cost?
faq.answer: Order volume, followed closely by chip security tier. Moving from a 500-1,000 unit pilot order to a 50,000-100,000+ unit established-programme order typically reduces per-card cost 30-60%, independent of any change to chip or material — and that discount compounds with consolidating orders across properties/departments into fewer, larger purchase orders rather than many small ones. Chip tier is the second-largest lever: choosing a security tier that actually matches the threat model (rather than defaulting to whatever the incumbent supplier stocks) avoids paying a 3-6x premium for cryptography the application does not need, or conversely under-securing a deployment that does need it.

faq.question: Why do some suppliers quote much cheaper RFID cards for the same chip family?
faq.answer: A quote meaningfully below the reference ranges in this guide for an otherwise-identical spec is the most common early warning sign of counterfeit or grey-market chip silicon, not a manufacturing efficiency other suppliers have missed. This is a well-documented issue specifically for MIFARE Classic, where genuine NXP silicon through authorised distribution typically runs US$0.11-0.18 per inlay while 'too-good-to-be-true' open-market pricing around US$0.06-0.08 is a known signal for Fudan or Huahong clone die in NXP-printed packaging. For any access-control, hospitality or government deployment, verify chip origin rather than choosing on price alone.

faq.question: Does pre-encoding add much to card cost?
faq.answer: Pre-encoding (loading facility-specific keys or data during manufacturing rather than on-site) typically adds US$0.05-0.15 per card for partial pre-encoding and US$0.15-0.35 for full pre-encoding with key injection. At a mid-size volume (50,000 cards/year), full pre-encoding runs an incremental US$7,500-17,500/year — which most hospitality and access-control operators recover within a year through faster check-in/issuance throughput and reduced on-site encoder wear and IT overhead.

faq.question: Is a wood or polycarbonate card ever the cost-effective choice?
faq.answer: Yes, but the calculation is about total replacement economics, not just sticker price. A property or programme with a high card-loss/replacement rate and a low per-unit cost ceiling should stay on PVC or recycled PVC. A property with low replacement frequency, long issuance cycles and a brand positioning that supports the premium (boutique/luxury hospitality, executive badging, government or aviation ID) can find that a more durable, higher-cost material has a lower total cost over the card's actual service life, even though the per-unit price is 4-15x higher than virgin PVC.
